study.title: Isaiah 11 The Renew of Jesse, the righteous reign, and the return of the people
study.overview: Isaiah 11 presents a hope concentrated in the figure born of the lineage of Jesse: a ruler chosen by God, full of the Spirit of the LORD, who judges with righteousness and brings peace to his kingdom. The chapter advances from the description of this ideal king for images of reconciliation in creation, of the attraction of the nations to their dominion and, finally, of the restoration of the scattered people. The central message is that God has not abandoned his promise: he will bring forth a legitimate king and, through him, will gather and lead his people with power like the exodus, but on an even wider scale.

outline.title: The Renovo of Jesse and the King full of the Spirit
outline.explanation: The first verses announce a new sprout of the lineage of Jesse, indicating continuity of David's house despite his abduction. This ruler does not act by appearance, but with wisdom, fear of the LORD, righteousness to the poor and firmness against the wicked. His identity is marked by righteousness and fidelity.

outline.title: Comprehensive peace and knowledge of the Lord
outline.explanation: The images of animals in peaceful coexistence show a restored order, in which violence loses space. The chapter explains this peace as a result of the knowledge of the Lord filling the whole earth. The reign of Jesse's descendant attracts nations as a banner raised by God.

outline.title: Restoration of the scattered and new exodus
outline.explanation: God again extends his hand to gather the rest of his people from many regions. The divided tribes cease to rival, and the Lord paves the way for the return of exile through images that resemble the crossing of the sea in the exodus. The past of Egypt's liberation serves as a model for the future meeting of the people.

study.context: The chapter binds to previous promises about a royal son and the contrast between the corruption of human rulers and the reign that God will set. The notes provided associate the Messianic hope with the environment of crisis and exile: the survival of the Davidic lineage seems almost interrupted, but God preserves the continuity of the promise. Also appears the exodus as a pattern of hope, that is, the memory of the liberation of Egypt is used as an image for a new divine intervention in favor of its people.
study.theology: Theologically, Isaiah 11 unites messianism, justice, peace and restoration. The promised king is not only a political leader; he is anointed by the Spirit, able to discern, rule and judge with equity. The chapter also teaches that true peace is born not only from human agreements, but also from the knowledge of God and from the sovereign action of the LORD on creation and upon the nations. Moreover, the restoration of the scattered people shows that God acts to gather the rest of their inheritance, healing internal divisions and overcoming historical obstacles. In evangelical Christian reading, this picture is culminatingly fulfilled in the Messiah, Jesus, as the commentators emphasizes; yet, the text itself emphasizes the hope of a just reign that produces reconciliation and return.

scholarViews.insight: The sprout of Jesse's cut trunk points to the continuity of David's royal lineage, even after appearing almost extinct, and the commentators understand this as final fulfillment in the Messiah.
The prophecy passes from temporal liberation to the great salvation in Christ, and the chapter introduces here the Messiah as the prince who arises from the house of David.
The image of the wolf with the lamb and the other beasts in peace depicts the renewal of an era of harmony, in which violence is removed and creation is presented as pacified.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to seek a king who judges not according to appearance, but according to the righteousness of God?
How does the peace described in the chapter depend on the knowledge of the Lord, and not just external changes?
How does the image of the new exodus correct our tendency to think that God no longer acts with the same power of the past?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to wait in the government of Christ and to align his own life with his character. In practice, this involves rejecting superficial judgments, defending the poor and the humble, promoting reconciliation rather than rivalry and remembering that God still brings together his people. It also invites you to read the current crises in the light of God's faithfulness: what seems like a cut torso can be the place where it brings forth hope. The concrete application is to cultivate prayer, justice and active trust in the Lord who leads his people along the path of return.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are partial; some explanations of commentators appear cut, especially in Matthew Henry, so the synthesis relies only on what was explicitly given. It is not possible to state historical details beyond what the notes support. Messianic identification is presented as an evangelical interpretation of the commentators, not as an independent factual statement of the text. Verse 16 resumes the image of the exodus, but the exact limits of its fulfillment remain interpretative.
